parts.title: The Nest
parts.summary: Aisle twenty-two is empty, but camera six still shows the man sitting there. Marcus finds a nest on the top shelf, with a notebook tracking all three of their shifts and Dana's alarm code. Camera six's clock is frozen at 4:37: someone looped the feed. Then the generator dies two days early, the fuel can is empty and still wet, and a voice behind you in the dark says not to open the bay door. Nobody's there.
script: Aisle twenty-two is empty. But on Dana's screen, he's still sitting there.
Your radio crackles. "He's right in front of you," Dana says. "He hasn't moved."
You're standing on the exact spot. Nothing but crumbs and a torn bag.
Marcus looks up. On the top shelf, twenty feet up, a sleeping bag hangs over the edge.
He climbs. "Somebody's been living up here," Marcus says. "For weeks."
Canned food. A flashlight. Store hoodies with the tags still on.
And a notebook. He drops it down to you.
Inside are three columns. Dana. Marcus. And a drawing of your orange beanie.
Every shift you've worked since October. Under Dana's name, four numbers. "That's my alarm code," she whispers.
Back at the office, camera six still shows him. Same spot. Same bag.
Dana leans in. The clock in the corner of the feed isn't moving. Four thirty-seven. Frozen.
"Someone looped it," Marcus says. "We've been watching a recording."
Then the generator coughs twice, and the whole store goes black.
"That's two days early," Dana says. "Somebody drained it."
Your flashlight finds the fuel can. Tipped over. Empty. Still wet.
Whoever did it was here a minute ago. And they're still inside.
Then a voice, right behind you in the dark. "Don't open the bay door."
You spin around. Your light hits the racking. Nobody's there.

parts.title: Ray
parts.summary: You spring the trap in aisle twenty-two and catch the stowaway: Ray. He confesses to living in the nest since October, looping camera six, and draining the generator so the lights wouldn't betray them from the road. Midway, he drops the real bomb — he used to work here, knew Dana before she was manager. At two in the morning, three heavy knocks hammer the buried bay door. Ray whispers the truck crew has arrived.

end_card.title: PART 4
end_card.hook: Who is prying the bay door open?

script: The stowaway drops from the ceiling into your arms.
You and Marcus wait in pitch black, flashlights killed.
Dana stares at the monitor. Camera six still loops the empty nest.
A shadow falls. Marcus snags him mid-drop. "Got you, bastard."
The man gasps, hood yanked back. Gray-green fabric, days of stubble.
"Ray," Dana's voice cracks over the radio. "His name is Ray."
You cinch zip ties on his wrists. He doesn't flinch.
"The lights could be seen from the road," he says. "Had to kill them."
"From who?" you ask. He clamps his mouth shut.
Dana's beam finds the notebook. "You knew my alarm code."
Ray smiles, exhausted. "I used to work here. Before you."
"Day manager, twenty nineteen," he says. "I stocked nights. You yelled at me for stacking apples wrong."
Dana goes pale. "You're the one who vanished."
"Didn't vanish. Got evicted. Came back to the only roof I knew."
The wall clock clicks past two in the morning.
Three slow knocks hammer the buried bay door.
Metal screams. The door shudders upward an inch.
Ray's eyes lock on yours. "They found us."

parts.title: Wake Up
parts.summary: You doze off on the train home after a long day and wake somewhere wrong: a silent car of motionless passengers, black windows, stops you've never heard of, and a phone stuck at 2:14. An old woman across the aisle is horrified to see you, introduces herself as June and gives you a handwritten list of nine rules. The passengers copy your movements until you freeze; a man in a red tracksuit laughs it off; the conductor punches your ticket. June's own ticket has been punched hundreds of times.

end_card.title: PART 2
end_card.hook: How long has June been riding?

script: You finally get on the train after a long day. All you want is takeout and your bed.
The second you sit down, the fatigue hits. Four more stops. A small nap couldn't hurt.
If only you knew how wrong you'd be.
You wake up to silence. Just the clack of the tracks.
The car is full, but nobody moves. Every passenger hides behind a newspaper.
Your phone says two fourteen in the morning. No signal.
Outside the windows, nothing. Just black.
The route map above the doors lists stops you've never heard of.
Across the aisle, an old woman knits a red scarf so long it trails across the floor.
She's the only one not reading. She's watching you.
When your eyes meet, her needles stop. Her face falls.
"Oh no," she whispers. "Not another one."
"Where are we?" you ask.
"I'm so sorry, sweetheart," she says. "I'm June. Listen to me very carefully."
She presses a folded sheet of paper into your hands.
"Read it," June says. "And do exactly what it says."
Rule one. Do not make eye contact with the other passengers.
Rule two. When the conductor asks for your ticket, smile. Do not speak.
Rule three. If the lights go out, keep your eyes closed until the doors chime.
Rule four. Never go into the last car.
Rule five. If someone calls your name, it isn't them.
Rule six. Your stop is the one that shows your name on the map. Get off, no matter what is on the platform.
Rule seven. Do not fall asleep again.
Rule eight. If your reflection blinks before you do, look away.
Rule nine. If the passengers start copying you, freeze.
You look up. Every newspaper is down. Every passenger is staring at you.
You lift a hand to rub your eyes. Every hand in the car lifts too.
Rule nine. You freeze.
Then the newspapers rustle back up, all at once.
Two rows down, a man in a red tracksuit laughs. "This is a prank show, right?"
He yanks at the doors. They don't budge.
Then, from the end of the car: click. Click.
A very tall conductor is coming down the aisle, punching tickets. His cap hides his eyes, but not his smile.
He stops at your seat. "Ticket, please."
There's a ticket in your pocket you don't remember buying.
Rule two. You smile and say nothing.
Click. He punches it and moves on.
June stares at the hole. The color drains from her face.
She holds up her own ticket. It's punched so many times it looks like lace.
"One hole," she whispers, "for every stop you miss."
Your ticket has one hole.
Hers has hundreds.
